title: No crime in Peel police shooting of D'Andre Campbell: SIU
article: Ontario's police watchdog says no crime was committed in the April shooting death of a Brampton man by Peel Regional Police.

The Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said Monday they found no reasonable grounds to criminally charge the Peel cop who shot 26-year-old D'Andre Campbell on April 6 - ruling the officer's actions as self-defence.

"I have little doubt that the SO (subject officer) believed he was acting in self-defence, and perhaps in defence of his partner, (Witness Officer no. 2), when he discharged his firearm at Mr. Campbell," wrote SIU director Joseph Martino in his report.
Officers had arrived at the Sawston Circle home around 5:30 p.m. after Campbell called 911 during a dispute with his parents.
The two responding officers found Campbell inside the kitchen brandishing a large knife. He advanced on police instead of complying with orders to drop his weapon.
"When he had neared to within a metre or so of the SO, the officer fired his CEW (conductive energy weapon) twice," Martino wrote.
The subject officer then attempted to disarm Campbell as the witness officer again fired his Taser, with no effect.
Campbell got back onto his feet with the knife, prompting both officers to draw their firearms.
"Within seconds, the SO fired his weapon twice in rapid succession, striking Mr. Campbell in the abdomen," wrote Martino.
Despite life-saving efforts, Campbell was pronounced dead by paramedics at 6:01 p.m.
The officers, Martino wrote, were let in by Campbell's mother and were therefore lawfully placed inside the home.
He also believes Campbell grabbed the knife as a weapon - countering claims by Campbell's family that he had been preparing food prior to police arrival.
Martino said Campbell's refusal to drop the knife convinced officers he posed a threat to themselves and his family - but added police could have done more to deescalate the situation.

"Though they knew that Mr. Campbell suffered from mental illness and was likely in an agitated condition, they did not confer with each other about the approach they would take once inside the home," Martino wrote.
Campbell's schizophrenia and bipolar disorder resulted in several police visits over the years - including two separate Mental Health Act apprehensions after calls by concerned family members.
Peel top cop Nishan Duraiappah reiterated his sorrow over the death, and acknowledged ongoing gaps in the system.

"While the SIU investigation found that under extraordinary circumstances our officers acted lawfully, in accordance with their training and responsibilities, we will continue to develop training and programs, and partner with mental health experts to ensure that individuals receive the right services, at the right time," the chief said in a statement Monday.
